edits.note: FOUR HITS IN ONE FILE, the batch's densest, and all four the same reading- or discussion-duration shape. 'Students revisit the text independently to check one answer they are unsure about' is self-bounding
the prompt is named in full before it; the board list closes it
'study the five-panel picture story silently' is bounded by the panels themselves — five — and by the eliciting that follows
the four charted answers (large-print notes, reading aloud, sitting nearer the board, describing pictures) are the real shape of this band

periods.activity_title: First Reading of the Informational Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Read (pp. 55–57): teacher-led read-aloud of the Braille text including new vocabulary.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces Louis Braille by asking students if they have ever seen or touched a Braille book, building curiosity about how reading without sight is possible.

Let us Read (pp. 55–57): teacher reads the informational text aloud expressively, pausing at key moments — Louis's accident, his arrival in Paris, his encounter with Night Writing — to allow students to follow along.
Teacher points to the Braille alphabet diagram on p. 56 and walks students through the raised-dot patterns for a few letters, inviting them to trace the dots with a finger on the page.

Teacher introduces the new words blacksmith, blind, pincushions, and invented — writing each on the board, reading it aloud with the class, and using the sentence context from the text to clarify meaning.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage may find the concept of tactile reading unfamiliar; grounding the text encounter in the concrete Braille diagram on p. 56 helps make the idea vivid. The final line — 'Thus, a blind person taught the world to see' — is worth reading slowly a second time; let the weight of it settle before moving on.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p. 58): three short-answer questions on the Braille text — describing the alphabet, Night Writing's failure, Louis's contribution.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads a short passage from the text aloud again (pp. 55–57), focusing on the section about Night Writing and Louis Braille's invention, so the content is fresh for discussion.

Let us Think A (p. 58): teacher poses the first two questions orally — what the Braille alphabet looks like, and why Night Writing failed — and takes paired responses before drawing out a class answer.

Let us Think A (p. 58): the third question — what Louis Braille did to make reading easier for the blind — is discussed as a class; teacher writes key phrases of the agreed answer on the board and students copy into their notebooks.
Students revisit the text independently to check one answer they are unsure about, then teacher conducts a quick round of oral sharing to confirm understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the full informational text together, students are ready to move from surface recall to organising what they understood into answers. A common difficulty is distinguishing Night Writing (Barbier's complex system) from Braille (Louis's simplified alphabet) — keeping the contrast clear on the board while discussing Question 2 prevents conflation.

periods.activity_title: Discussion — Blindness, the White Cane, and a World Without Light

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p. 58): guided discussion on the white cane and imagining a day without light.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking if any student has seen a person with blindness walking with a white cane, and what the student noticed, creating a bridge from the text's theme to personal observation.

Let us Think B (p. 58): teacher poses the white-cane question to the class — why is the cane white? — and facilitates a guided conversation; teacher draws out ideas about visibility, signalling, and road safety.

Let us Think B (p. 58): teacher poses the second prompt — imagine a day the world goes dark; what difficulties might you face? — students discuss in pairs, then share with the class; teacher lists difficulties on the board.

Teacher invites three or four students to give a one-sentence summary of what surprised them most in the discussion, and closes by connecting the imagined difficulties back to Louis Braille's lifelong experience.

periods.teacher_notes: The white-cane question often surprises students who have not thought beyond colour; guide them to the idea that white is a high-visibility warning signal to drivers and pedestrians rather than a decoration. The dark-world prompt is deliberately imaginative — allow unexpected difficulties (finding food, calling for help, travelling) and accept all thoughtful responses.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak (pp. 58–59): close-eyes touch activity — feel an object and describe it aloud using sentence frames.
Let us Listen (p. 59): teacher reads 'spl' consonant-cluster words; students listen and repeat.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to close their eyes briefly and place their hands flat on the desk, noticing only what their hands can tell them — texture, temperature, shape — preparing them for the object-description task.

Let us Speak (pp. 58–59): teacher instructs students to close their eyes, pick one small object from their bag or pencil case, feel it, and then put it away; students complete the three sentence frames on p. 58 orally with a partner, then add two more descriptive lines of their own and share with the class.

Let us Listen (p. 59): teacher reads each word — spoon, splinter, spin, splash, speak, split, space, splendid — clearly and slowly three to four times, stressing the consonant cluster; class repeats as a group after each reading, then in pairs.

Teacher writes 'spl', 'sp', and 'spl' on the board, says a word from the set, and asks students to hold up one finger if they hear 'sp' and two fingers if they hear 'spl', consolidating sound discrimination before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The touch-and-describe activity directly enacts how Louis Braille's world was built on touch — naming this connection briefly grounds the activity in the chapter's theme without turning it into a lecture. Some students may struggle to add two original descriptive lines; accept shape, weight, texture, or temperature as equally valid descriptive dimensions.
materials: Small classroom objects (pen, eraser, sharpener, coin — any available)

periods.activity_title: Writing Words in Braille Using Dot Patterns

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write A (p. 60): write words Cat, Man, Boy, Jug and own name using Braille dot patterns (bindis).

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the textbook to the Braille alphabet diagram on p. 56, walks the class through the dot-cell structure — six positions in two columns of three — and demonstrates on the board how 'C' and 'A' are formed before students attempt the task.
Let us Write A (p. 60): teacher models the completed example (shown in the textbook) on the board, then guides students through 'Cat' together, dot by dot, before students continue independently.
Students work through Man, Boy, and Jug on p. 60, using bindis or drawn dot circles; teacher circulates, checks dot placement against the alphabet chart, and gives immediate feedback.

Students write their own names in Braille; teacher invites two or three students to display their name-cards and the class tries to decode them using the chart on p. 56, making the task communicative.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often mix up letters with visually similar dot patterns (e.g., 'a' and 'b'); circulating with the Braille alphabet chart visible makes correction faster. Giving each student bindis or asking them to draw small filled circles works equally well — the physical marking of dots is what matters.
materials: Bindis or pencils and small stickers

periods.activity_title: Writing a List — Eye Safety Precautions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write B (p. 61): plan and write a list of precautions to protect eyes from harm.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the prompt aloud from p. 61 — the context of Louis losing his eyesight in an accident and the newspaper report about a child's firecracker injury — and asks students to name two situations in which eyes can be hurt, recording ideas on the board.

Planning phase: teacher guides a whole-class brainstorm of precautions (goggles when working with sharp objects, keeping away from fireworks, not reading in dim light, washing hands before touching eyes); teacher writes the class list on the board.

Let us Write B (p. 61): students draft their own lists independently — at least four precautions in complete sentences; teacher circulates, offering brief sentence-frame support ('We should always…', 'It is important to…') to students who need it.

Pairs swap notebooks and read each other's lists; each partner checks that the precautions are written as complete sentences and marks any unclear ones with a question mark; teacher takes one or two volunteers to read aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: This writing task is designed to begin and end within this unit — planning, drafting, and peer review are all completed here. Students who finish quickly can add a title and a brief opening sentence to their list, giving it the shape of a short advisory note.

periods.activity_title: Past Continuous Tense — Rule and Sentence Transformation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn C (pp. 61–62): understand was/were + verb-ing rule; transform six present-continuous sentences to past.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the three example sentences from pp. 61–62 on the board — including the sentence about Louis Braille playing near his home — and asks students what they notice about the verbs; guides them to see the 'was/were + action word + ing' pattern.

Teacher explains the rule: 'was' for one person, animal, or bird; 'were' for more than one; writes four or five quick examples from classroom life on the board and students call out the correct form together.

Let us Learn C (pp. 61–62): students work through the six transformation sentences — dogs barking, Grandfather searching, Sheeba writing, he singing, we playing, the man pushing — writing each in their notebooks; teacher checks the first two with the whole class before students complete the rest.

Teacher selects four sentences at random and calls on individual students to read the transformed sentence aloud; classmates signal thumbs-up or thumbs-down, and teacher corrects any errors with brief explanation.

periods.teacher_notes: The sentence about the man pushing his wheelchair and the one about Grandfather searching for spectacles give opportunities to mention everyday situations involving people with disabilities or age-related difficulties — connecting the grammar work to the chapter's theme of empathy. Watch for students who write 'were' for singular subjects when the noun sounds like a group word (e.g., 'team') — the rule at this stage is straightforwardly count-based.

periods.activity_title: Past Continuous in Context — Picture-Story Fill-in

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn D (pp. 62–63): fill blanks in Tarandeep's picture story using the correct past-continuous forms from the box.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to open their textbooks to pp. 62–63 and study the five-panel picture story silently; teacher then asks what is happening in each panel, eliciting oral responses to activate the vocabulary before reading the passage.

Teacher reads the Tarandeep passage aloud, pausing at each blank and asking students to predict which option from the box fits — 'Is Tarandeep doing one action or many? Singular or plural subject?' — before moving on.
Let us Learn D (pp. 62–63): students complete all six blanks independently in their notebooks; teacher circulates and notes common errors for group correction.

Teacher reads each sentence stem aloud; class calls out the answer together; teacher writes the correct form on the board and briefly explains any blank where more than two students gave a wrong answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the transformation rule in the previous word-work activity, students are now applying the same structure to a connected narrative — the shift from isolated sentences to a story context is the key pedagogical step here. The picture story is integral: students who look at the panels before choosing an option are much less likely to confuse 'was feeding' with 'was scattering' — prompt them to use the pictures actively.

periods.activity_title: Feel and Identify — Making a Tactile Impression

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p. 64): press a shape into paper with a pencil back; close eyes and identify the raised surface by touch.

homework.task_brief: Let us Explore (p. 64): find out about the nearest resource centre for people with blindness and write two sentences about what you discover.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits how Louis Braille's system works — raised dots felt by running a finger across the page — and tells students they will experience a simplified version of tactile reading during this unit.

Let us Do (p. 64): teacher demonstrates pressing a circle into paper using the back of a pencil; students press a circle, a plus sign, and one letter of their choice into their own paper, pressing firmly on a hard surface.

Students close their eyes, flip their paper over, and run a finger across the raised surface; teacher asks them to identify what they pressed; students then swap papers with a partner and try to identify the partner's shape by touch alone.

Quick sharing circle: teacher asks who could identify every shape correctly, who identified some, and who found it difficult; students briefly discuss what made identification easier or harder, connecting their experience to what Braille readers do with every word.

periods.teacher_notes: The physical experience of identifying shapes by touch — especially a partner's paper — gives students a concrete, memorable sense of the tactile world that Louis Braille systematised. If white clay is available, a small group can try impressing letters into it as an extension; if not, paper and pencil-back work perfectly well.

periods.activity_title: Empathy in Action — Supporting Classmates with Low Vision

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore (p. 64): discuss how classmates can assist children with low vision; share ideas and examples.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the prompt aloud from p. 64 and asks students if they know or have seen a classmate who holds a book very close to their eyes or wears thick glasses; the teacher explains what low vision means without naming anyone, building empathy and awareness.

Let us Explore (p. 64): students discuss in pairs — what can a friend do to help a classmate with low vision? — then share with the class; teacher lists ideas on the board (large-print notes, reading aloud, sitting nearer the board, describing pictures).

Teacher adds one or two ideas that students did not think of (describing illustrations in books, pairing up during outdoor activities), and facilitates a brief discussion on why these acts matter — connecting to the chapter's theme that small acts can open the world to someone.

Each student writes two sentences in their notebook: one thing they will do for a classmate who needs help seeing, and one thing they learnt from Louis Braille's story; two or three students share aloud before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks students to move from knowing about Braille to acting with empathy — the brief written reflection at the end anchors that shift personally. The sentence writing is not a new writing task but a short personal response that takes the chapter's final idea off the page and into the student's own thinking.

items.source_lo: Student reads and extracts key information using an informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Louis Braille's life, his accident, Night Writing, and the invention of the Braille alphabet.
items.item_stem: Captain Charles Barbier de la Serre invented a system called 'Night Writing' so that soldiers could read messages in the dark. Why was this system not widely adopted?

options.label: A
options.text: It could only be used by soldiers, not by civilians.

options.label: B
options.text: It required special paper that was difficult to find.

options.label: C
options.text: It used letters instead of dots, making it hard to feel.

options.label: D
options.text: It was too complex for most people to use easily.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may think Night Writing's limitation was about who could access it, rather than how difficult the system itself was.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may be confusing Night Writing's raised dots-and-dashes with ordinary printed letters, missing the detail about complexity.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student is guessing a practical barrier not mentioned in the text, rather than drawing on the stated reason.

items.item_stem: The informational text says that Louis Braille lost his sight as a very young child and went on to create a reading system used around the world. In one to three sentences, explain what Louis Braille created and how it works.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Louis Braille created the Braille alphabet — a system of raised dots where one dot pattern stands for each of the twenty-six letters of the English alphabet. It is read by running the fingers across the dots rather than by using the eyes.

items.item_stem:
Read each sentence. Decide whether the underlined verb form is correct or incorrect for the past continuous tense.
1. Long ago, Louis Braille were learning letters by touch at the Royal Institute.
2. The soldiers was reading secret messages in the dark using Night Writing.
3. Louis was working hard to simplify the raised-dot system for everyone.
4. The children were helping their friend find her way across the classroom.

options.text: Long ago, Louis Braille were learning letters by touch at the Royal Institute. — The verb form is correct.
Louis was working hard to simplify the raised-dot system for everyone. — The verb form is correct.
The children were helping their friend find her way across the classroom. — The verb form is correct.
The soldiers was reading secret messages in the dark using Night Writing. — The verb form is correct.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — Louis Braille is one person, so the correct form is 'was learning', not 'were learning'.  2. False — 'soldiers' is plural, so the correct form is 'were reading', not 'was reading'.  3. True — 'was working' is correct for a single subject.  4. True — 'were helping' is correct for a plural subject.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Louis was learning the Braille alphabet.  2. The blind children were reading books by touch.

items.visual_stimulus:
Situation | Helpful action
A classmate holds every book very close to her eyes to read. | Read the question aloud for her so she can follow along.
A classmate cannot see the writing on the board clearly from the back row. | Bring a printout with larger letters to share during reading time.
A classmate cannot read a question on the printed worksheet easily. | Help him move to a seat nearer the front of the classroom.

answer_key.right: Bring a printout with larger letters to share during reading time.

items.item_stem: Louis Braille created a way for people with blindness to read and write using only their sense of touch. Think about a classmate or neighbour who has low vision. Tell the class two specific things you could do — at school or at home — to make their daily life a little easier. Explain why each thing would help.

expected_elements: Names two concrete, specific helpful actions.
Explains clearly why each action helps.
Shows awareness of the other person's experience.
